> nimble_model <- nimbleModel(code = nimblemodel,
>                             constants = list(mu_lam1 = mu_lam1,

>                                              nscale = nscale),

I also have four environmental variable that I would like to use as predictor using their values and understand what scale is best explaining. The scales are 250m,500,1000 and 2000m.

> > Thanks Heather for contributing on this. Frank, let me suggest how we can get to the bottom of this. In a case like this, we are mostly going to look at your code in terms of software mechanics rather than statistical meaning (but sometimes that), so that is what I am trying to follow. When you had X_det set up as five dimensional and used it as two dimensional, it was hard for me to guess what you were trying to do. Now you have tried using X_det as five dimensional in the model and you reported that it's still not working, so we will need to see that to try to figure out what is going on. What really can work well is if you can reduce the context of the problem by cutting away parts of the model are not related (i.e. remove as much as you can so it is as simple as possible to demonstrate the problem) and providing a completely reproducible example (meaning that we can run your code and reproduce the error you are seeing). Often a good way to do that is to provide code to simulate relevant data, and that is easier to do once you have removed parts of your model that are not relevant to the problem. So if you can make such a minimal reproducible example and send it, then people on the list can run your code and make suggestions.
> > Fingers crossed we can get things sorted out for you.

messages.subject: Re: Error message
messages.body_plain:
The error I get at the nimbleModel step is:

indexing error found for model variable(s): count_array ; please check that variables used for indexing are properly defined in the relevant for loop(s)

In the code, I see

        count_array[v, t, , ss_trunc, i] ~ dpois(lambda[v, t, i])

Only a scalar can follow a Poisson (or any scalar) distribution, so you'll need a value for the third index of count_array. Leaving it blank would indicate a vector, which can't follow a Poisson.

There is another problem. ss is stochastic, from which ss_trunc is calculated and then used as an index for count_array. We would call this a stochastic index or more generally a dynamic index. The index will change during MCMC sampling, for example. However, a dynamic index can only be used on the right-hand side of a declaration. It can't really make sense on the left-hand side such as here.  I am not quickly grasping what the intended modeling idea is with that.

Perry

messages.subject: Error in 1 %.s% 10
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
After seeing Perry's talk at TWS, I thought I'd try out nimbleHMC for my continuous nodes, Installing and loading the library worked great. However, when I try to build the MCMC, I get the error:

"One or more errors occurred looking for variables in a model (first 10 shown below).
These messages may be cryptic, but generally the variable or expression somewhere in each message was not valid in a model:
Error in 1 %.s% 10 : could not find function "%.s%"
Error in 1 %.s% 10 : could not find function "%.s%"
Error in 1 %.s% 10 : could not find function "%.s%"
Error in 1 %.s% 10 : could not find function "%.s%"
Error in 1 %.s% 10 : could not find function "%.s%"
Error in 1 %.s% 10 : could not find function "%.s%"
Error in 1 %.s% 10 : could not find function "%.s%"
Error in 1 %.s% 10 : could not find function "%.s%"
Error in 1 %.s% 10 : could not find function "%.s%"
Error in 1 %.s% 10 : could not find function "%.s%""

Prior to this error, I have setup the model steps via:
prepnim <- nimbleModel(code = cwd_mod, constants = consts, dat = dat,
                       inits = inits, calculate = T)
mcmcnim <- configureMCMC(prepnim, monitors = params, print = T)
mcmcnim$removeSampler('survivors')
mcmcnim$removeSampler(paste0('n[1:12, ', 2:consts$nocc, ', 1:24, ', rep(1:3, each = consts$nocc), ']')) #adjust the 24 to reflect pixel count
for(i in 1:consts$nState){
  for(j in 2:consts$nocc){
    for(k in 1:consts$nPix){
      for(b in 1:3){
      mcmcnim$addSampler(target = c(paste0('n[1:12, ', j, ', 1:24, ', b, ']'), paste0('survivors[', i, ", ", j, ", ", k, ", ", b, "]")),
                         type = 'mymultiSampler1step',
                         control = list(tries = 5, t = j, s = i, q = k, b =b, nPix = consts$nPix,
                                        nState = consts$nState, nocc = consts$nocc, pixcount = consts$pixcount,
                                        pixopts = consts$pixopts), silent = TRUE)
      } #end b
    } #end k
  } #end j
}
nuts_compat <- c('p_obs', 's.r','beta0', 'c0', 'c1', paste0('beta1[', 1:12, ']'),paste0('phi0[', 1:12, ']'))
mcmcnim$removeSampler(nuts_compat)
addHMC(mcmcnim, target = nuts_compat) #use HMC for continuous variables
nimMCMC <- buildMCMC(mcmcnim) #actually build the code for those samplers

I thought at first this error was because of something being incompatible with the nodes I selected, but after looking at the dependencies for those nodes, that shouldn't be the case. My current theory is that nimbleHMC doesn't like either my custom sampler (which does not directly interact with the nodes I'd like to run through HMC) or the presence of the multinomials elsewhere in the code.

Or maybe it's none of those!

Any suggestions?

-Heather

Code/data/functions attached. I apologize for their complexity.

messages.subject: Re: Cross Categorization Model with Joint Dirichlet Distributions in NIMBLE?
messages.subject_clean: Cross Categorization Model with Joint Dirichlet Distributions in NIMBLE?
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the quick response, Chris! Most of the changes you mention were alterations I made when my model code was initially failing, but I forgot to remove them after trying them out. The original code I had was structured as follows:

fake_data <- data.frame(response_id=1:170)
for(q in 1:120) {
  fake_data[,paste("Q", q, sep="")] <- sample(1:7, 170, replace = TRUE)
}

code <- nimbleCode({
  z[1:N] ~ dCRP(alpha1, size = N)
  alpha1 ~ dgamma(1, 1)
  y[1:Q] ~ dCRP(alpha2, size = Q)
  alpha2 ~ dgamma(1, 1)

  alphas[1:7] <- rep(1, 7)

  for(i in 1:M) {
    for(j in 1:R) {
      thetas[i, j, 1:7] ~ ddirch(alphas[1:7])
    }
  }

for(i in 1:N) {

    r[i, 1] <- i
    for(j in 1:Q) {

      r[i, (j+1)] ~ dcat(thetas[z[i], y[j], 1:7])
    }
  }

})

set.seed(1)
constants <- list(N = 169, M = 10, Q = 117, R = 10)
data <- list(r=fake_data)
init_thetas <- array(dim=c(constants$M, constants$R, 7))
for(i in 1:constants$M) {
  for(j in 1:constants$R) {
    init_thetas[i, j, 1:7] <- rdirichlet(1, c(1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1))
  }
}
inits <- list(thetas = init_thetas,
              z = sample(1:10, size = constants$N, replace = TRUE),
              y = sample(1:10, size = constants$Q, replace = TRUE),
              alpha1  = 1, alpha2 = 1)
model <- nimbleModel(code, constants, data, inits)

# cmodel <- compileNimble(model)

monitors <- c('z', 'y')
nimbleOptions(MCMCusePredictiveDependenciesInCalculations = TRUE)
modelConf <- configureMCMC(model, print=TRUE, useConjugacy=FALSE, monitors = monitors)
modelMCMC <- buildMCMC(modelConf)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Heather,

Ok I took a careful look (and yes saw that you do have the buildDerivs in your code) and it appears that you have revealed a bug in the steps that determine what pieces of model variables are needed to use the AD (automatic differentiation) system.
The problem arises from the distinct way that you have n[1:nState,t,q,b] being split into pieces on the right-hand side of these declarations:

        n_post[1, t, q,b] ~ dpois(sum(n[1:nState,t,q,b]*c_repro[1:nState,1])*s.r) # neg female fawns
        n_post[2,t,q,b] <- n[2,t,q,b]
        n_post[3,t,q,b] <- n[3,t,q,b]
        n_post[4, t, q,b] ~ dpois(sum(n[1:nState,t,q,b]*c_repro[1:nState,4])*s.r) # pos female fawns
        n_post[5,t,q,b] <- n[5,t,q,b]
        n_post[6,t,q,b] <- n[6,t,q,b]

That should work but doesn't. Here are a couple of workaround ideas until we can offer some kind of fix:

1.  You could break up n into four different variables, like n_neg_female, n_pos_female, etc., each with the first index running from 1:3. I think this would avoid the problem created in your current code.

2. You could rearrange the ordering of the first index in n (and, for sanity, I assume n_post as well) such that the 4 dpois statements are contiguous and then the 8 elements of n used deterministically are contiguous in n.   E.g.

       n_post[1, t, q,b] ~ dpois(sum(n[1:nState,t,q,b]*c_repro[1:nState,1])*s.r) # neg female fawns
        n_post[2, t, q,b] ~ dpois(sum(n[1:nState,t,q,b]*c_repro[1:nState,4])*s.r) # pos female fawns
        <... 3 and 4>
        n_post[5,t,q,b] <- n[5,t,q,b]
        n_post[6,t,q,b] <- n[6,t,q,b]
        n_post[7,t,q,b] <- n[7,t,q,b]
        n_post[8,t,q,b] <- n[8,t,q,b]
       < etc...>

I realize that might confuse and complicate interpretations later, but I'm just saying I think it would avoid the problem.

Thanks for sharing your code. I hope one of these workarounds is feasible for you to keep you moving in the short term.

Perry

> hi Brennan,
>
> Thanks for the follow up and the additional testing.
>
> It looks like there is another related, but distinct, numerical issue that can come up in this case. What I am seeing is that when one of the two `ab[i,1:2]` values gets close to zero, numerical underflow can cause a sampled value of `theta[i,1:2]` (from its conjugate Dirichlet distribution) to be exactly (1,0) (or (0,1)). Then if that `theta[i,1:2]` is the only member of its cluster, when the CRP sampling goes to sample a new value for `z[i]`, it's possible that the log probability density value for `theta[i,1:2]` under the other clusters are all -Inf. And using the non-conjugate CRP sampler to sample `alpha[i]` and `beta[i,1:2]` values for a new cluster will generally give values that also have -Inf for the log probability density value for `theta[i,1:2]`. At that point, the CRP sampler is trying to decide between the various possible new values for `z[i]` with all the log probabilities being -Inf and the crash occurs.
>
> This is a tricky situation. We can of course (and will at a minimum in our upcoming release) error trap this and produce an error message rather than a crash.
>
> However, I am not seeing a good way around the numerical problems. It's not clear to me there is a way to sample `z[i]` when `theta[i,1:2]` is (1,0) in a way that retains the validity of the MCMC sampling (i.e., I don't think sampling uniformly from the possible `z[i]` values is correct). And I don't see a reasonable way to avoid getting exact (1,0) values in the conjugate sampling of `theta[i,1:2]`.
>
> For your case, one possible work-around (if you will generally have only two elements of theta) is that you could specify theta[i] using a beta distribution and, as needed, use truncation to ensure it never is sampled as exactly 0 or 1:
>
> theta[i] ~ T(dbeta(ab[i,1],ab[i,2]), .001, .999)
>
> You could also think about using the stickbreaking representation rather than the CRP.  That might avoid the issue. Or it seems that in the paper you reference, they used some other sampling strategies based on drawing from the prior.
>
> I will try to think more about this to see if there is a better numerical solution on our end.
>
> -chris

Hello Chris,

On Thursday, October 31, 2024 at 4:56:54 PM UTC+2 Chris Paciorek wrote:
> Hi Etienne,
>
> A follow-up on this. I mis-diagnosed the problem in the original setting. It's not the `dcat` statements, but rather that the result of the stochastic indexing is a vector rather than a scalar. Our AD system doesn't support that. We'll make some changes to the system to error trap this and give an informative error message.
>
> There's some discussion of the issue in this GitHub issue <https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/issues/1500>.
>
> A work-around is that if you do want to use AD with your model, you could do the stochastic indexing one-by-one, like this:
>
> gammaTmp[i,j,1:2] <- c(gamma[z[i,j-1],1] gamma[z[i,j-1],2])
> z[i,j] ~ dcat(gammaTmp[i,j,1:2])
> omegaTmp[i,j, 1:2] <- c(omega[z[i,j],1], omega[z[i,j],2])
> y[i,j] ~ dcat(omegaTmp[i,j,1:2])
>
> Or if the vector was long, you could have a loop instead of using `c`, illustrated here only for `gammaTmp`:
> for(k in 1:K)
>    gammaTmp[i,j,k] <- gamma[z[i,j-1],k]
>
> You might also be able to make use of the discrete hidden Markov model distributions in the nimbleEcology package.
>
> -chris
>
> On Thu, Oct 24, 2024 at 4:46 AM Etienne Sebag <etienn...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hello Chris,
> >
> > Thank you so much for your reply. I really appreciate it.
> >
> > I was now able to make MCEM work successfully without using AD for now.
> >
> > Have a great one,
> > Etienne.
> >
> > On Wednesday, October 23, 2024 at 7:31:29 PM UTC+3 Chris Paciorek wrote:
> > > Hi Etienne,
> > >
> > > This seems to be failing because of the derivative-building with discrete nodes in the model. Our AD system should allow such nodes, but somehow with the nested `dcat` nodes, there is a failure.
> > > I will file an issue for us to look into this.
> > >
> > > For now, if you want to use EM, you can leave out `buildDerivs = TRUE` and then follow the instructions in `help(buildMCEM)` to use MCEM without making use of automatic differentiation.
> > >
> > > -Chris
> > >
> > > On Tue, Oct 22, 2024 at 7:13 AM Etienne Sebag <etienn...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Hello everyone. I hope you are doing well.
> > > >
> > > > I am trying to run an MCEM (Monte Carlo Expectation Maximization) algorithm in Nimble using the command buildMCEM. The data generating mechanism is based off of this reading: https://oliviergimenez.github.io/banana-book/hmmcapturerecapture.html#marginalization under section 3.6. It is, in essence, a capture-recapture ecological framework and I want to estimate the survival probability phi and the detection probability p in an HMM.
> > > >
> > > >  I am using Windows,  and my R version is 4.4.1, and my Nimble version is 1.2.1. I am following this workflow to implement MCEM algorithm: https://r-nimble.org/nimbleExamples/pumpMCEM.html
> > > >
> > > >  The code for the data generating process is:
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >

messages.subject: Re: another question about NUTS
messages.body_plain:
Hi Qing,

This is a good question. I don't think there are general rules. Certainly updating all the continuous parameters via NUTS in one big block would be the standard way to do things and allows NUTS to account for all the possible dependence amongst the parameters. But you could consider using smaller blocks. Presumably you'd want the smaller blocks to not have much dependence between them.

-Chris

On Mon, Nov 4, 2024 at 2:36 PM Qing Zhao <white...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Dear Team,
>
> Now NUTS seems to work well for me, I'm considering what the best way is to use it. Thinking about Stan, I would assume that all the parameters are updated in one big block. Nimble allows us to group parameters and update them in different blocks, when using NUTS (but let me know if I got it wrong). That makes me wonder if I should simply swap NUTS in for all the continuous parameters in a model and update them in one big block. Are there any general rules for this? Thank you.
>
> Best,
> Qing

messages.subject: Re: Cross Categorization Model with Joint Dirichlet Distributions in NIMBLE?
messages.subject_clean: Cross Categorization Model with Joint Dirichlet Distributions in NIMBLE?
messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Thomas.

So, this model structure falls in a grey zone for our CRP sampling. Back when we had funding support for a researcher to work on implementing the CRP, we talked about handling this case, but we never quite got it all done.  I believe the error message you are getting is an overly cautious one. And that we could disable it and NIMBLE could do the sampling. However, it might not mix very well because it would not use conjugacy in sampling the new cluster memberships even if the conjugacy was present. (Working on that was what we hoped to do but did not have time to do.) Basically, when the sampling proposes a new cluster, it would use a 'nonconjugate' sampler that proposes new cluster parameters from their prior, rather than determining whether to open a new cluster based on the marginal probability (marginalizing over possible cluster parameter values) and then when opening a new cluster, determining the new cluster parameters by drawing from the conditional distribution given prior and data.

If you'd like to try it out with the nonconjugate approach, I could set you up with a branch of nimble that you could install from and you could experiment to see how well it works for your problem.

-chris

I believe the error message you are getting is an overly cautious one. And that we could disable it and NIMBLE could do the sampling. However, it might not mix very well because it would not use conjugacy in sampling the new cluster memberships even if the conjugacy was present. (Working on that was what we hoped to do but did not have time to do.) Basically, when the sampling proposes a new cluster, it would use a 'nonconjugate' sampler that proposes new cluster parameters from their prior, rather than determining whether to open a new cluster based on the marginal probability (marginalizing over possible cluster parameter values) and then when opening a new cluster, determining the new cluster parameters by drawing from the conditional distribution given prior and data.

messages.subject: BNP AR(1) model
messages.body_plain:
Hi, all!

I'm trying to fit a Bayesian nonparametric (BNP) AR(1) model to some simulated data. Below is my NIMBLE code. I'm having some trouble with the indexing in NIMBLE, and getting the following error in red after "modelMCMC <- buildMCMC(modelConf)":

code <- nimbleCode({

  # ordinal response
  for(i in 1:N){
    y[i] ~ dinterval(z[i], cut[])
  }

  # latent Gaussian variable
  z[1] ~ dnorm(mean=mu[1], var = s2)
  mu[1] <- beta0[1]+(beta1)*x[1]
  beta0[1] <- beta0tilde[u[1]]
  for(i in 2:N) {
    z[i] ~ dnorm(mean=mu[i], var = s2)
    mu[i] <- beta0[i]+(beta1)*x[i] + rho*(z[i-1] - (beta0[i-1]+(beta1)*x[i-1]))
    beta0[i] <- beta0tilde[u[i]]
  }

  # BNP
  u[1:N] ~ dCRP(alpha, size = N) # membership vector for BNP
  alpha ~ dgamma(1, 1)
  for(i in 1:M) {
    beta0tilde[i] ~ dnorm(0, var = 10)
  }
  s2 ~ dinvgamma(1, 1)
  beta1 ~ dnorm(0, var = 10)
  rho ~ dunif(0,1)
})

model <- nimbleModel(code, constants, data, inits)

cmodel <- compileNimble(model)

monitors <- c('u', 'beta0tilde', 'beta1', 's2' , 'alpha', 'rho')
modelConf <- configureMCMC(model, monitors = monitors)
modelMCMC <- buildMCMC(modelConf)

Error in samplerFunction(model = model, mvSaved = mvSaved, target = target,  :
  sampler_CRP: Detected unusual indexing in beta0tilde[u[1]] . NIMBLE's CRP MCMC sampling is not designed for this case.

Many thanks for any thoughts.

Best,

Mostafa.

messages.subject: Re: another question about NUTS
messages.body_plain:
Hi Qing, if there is no dependence between one parameter and the rest of the parameters, then yes, I'd expect a conjugate sampler to be the best choice for that parameter. But when there is dependence between that parameter and the others, that won't necessarily be the case, and the best choice will probably depend on the strength of the dependence. That's because the sampling for the one parameter will be constrained by the current values of the other parameters. So it can be better to use blocking and not to take advantage of conjugacy for the component parameters.

There can also be effects from the computational costs of the different potential samplers that affect what choice is best.

-Chris

Hi folks

hi Mostafa,

This check is in place to avoid us setting up incorrect sampling with model structures that nimble's CRP functionality doesn't expect. In this case that is because `u` is used in two different declarations. Please try to put the `beta0` declarations in their own for loop and see if it works:

```
for(i in 1:N)

  beta0[i] <- beta0tilde[u[i]]
 for(i in 2:N) {
    z[i] ~ dnorm(mean=mu[i], var = s2)
    mu[i] <- beta0[i]+(beta1)*x[i] + rho*(z[i-1] - (beta0[i-1]+(beta1)*x[i-1]))
  }

```

Let me know if there are further problems after that.

-chris

messages.subject: Re: Cross Categorization Model with Joint Dirichlet Distributions in NIMBLE?
messages.subject_clean: Cross Categorization Model with Joint Dirichlet Distributions in NIMBLE?
messages.body_plain:
hi Thomas,

Please try installing nimble from this branch I just made and see how it goes.

remotes::install_github("nimble-dev/nimble", ref = "allow_crossed_crp", subdir = "packages/nimble")

Because of the multiple indices, nimble is unable to smartly figure out when there are empty clusters for which it doesn't need to sample the cluster parameters (the thetas elements). So it will sample all M*R*7 thetas at every iteration. I see that you've already set M << N and R << Q, which will help to mitigate the problem. If you see the warning about exceeding the max number of clusters, you'll need to increase either M or R or both. (Since you have two CRPs, you'll need to experiment a bit to see which one you need to adjust.)

-chris

Hi all,
New NIMBLE user here. I am trying to vectorize the following code, and I am receiving an error (see below) when trying to index. Any help would be much appreciated!

My model is working well, but it takes 20+ hours to run, and I need it to run faster without sacrificing iterations.

library(nimble)
library(tidyverse)
library(mcmcplots)
library(MCMCvis)
library(ggplot2)
library(coda)
library(data.table)
library(loo)
source('attach.nimble_v2.R')

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(readr)

SSM_Ty <- nimbleCode({

  Sigma.obs ~ dexp(1) #T(dt(mu=0, sigma=1, df=1), 0, )

  hatch.effect ~ dnorm(mean=0,sd=5) #dt(mu=0, sigma=1, df=1)

  Sigma.proc ~ dexp(1)

  lambda ~ dt(mu=0, sigma=1, df=1)

  # Process Model

  for (t in 1:(n.years-1)) {

    lambda.year.RE <http://lambda.year.RE>[t]~dnorm(mean=0, sd=Sigma.proc)
    lambda.year[t] <- lambda + lambda.year.RE <http://lambda.year.RE>[t]

  }

  for (c in 1:n.colonies) {

    N.est[c,1] ~ dnorm(mean=5, sd=6.884395)

    for (t in 1:(n.years-1)) {

      N.est[c, t+1] <- N.est[c, t] + lambda.year[t]

    } # t process
  } # Colony loop

  # Observation Model (Likelihood)
  for (i in 1:n.obs) {

    N.exp[i] <- N.est[ColonyNo[i], Year[i]] + hatch.effect*stage[i]

    N[i] ~ dlnorm(meanlog=N.exp[i], sdlog=Sigma.obs)
  }

  for (t in 1:(n.years)) {

    N.all[t]<- sum(exp(N.est[1:n.colonies,t]))

  } # t loop

}) # SSM

# Parameters monitored
parameters <- c("N.est","lambda","Sigma.proc",
                "N.all", "Sigma.obs", "lambda.year", "hatch.effect", "logProb_N")

# MCMC Settings
ni <- 1000000
nt <- 50
nb <- 500000
nc <- 3

# Data
nimble.data = list(N=data$Count,
                   stage=as.numeric(as.factor(data$stage))-1)

nimble.constants = list(n.years = max(data$year)-min(data$year)+1,
                        n.colonies=length(unique(data$ColonyName2)),
                        ColonyNo=as.numeric(as.factor(data$ColonyName2)),
                        n.obs=length(data$Count),
                        Year=data$year-(min(data$year)-1))

mcmc.output_Ty <- nimbleMCMC(code = SSM_Ty,
                             data = nimble.data,
                             constants=nimble.constants,
                             monitors = parameters,
                             niter = ni,
                             nburnin = nb,
                             nchains = nc,
                             thin=nt,
                             summary=TRUE,
                             samplesAsCodaMCMC = TRUE)

attach.nimble(mcmc.output_Ty$samples)

  for (i in 1:n.obs) {

  }
    N.all[t:n.years]<- sum(exp(N.est[1:n.colonies,t:n.years]))

}) # SSM

Error in getSymbolicParentNodesRecurse(x, constNames, indexNames, nimbleFunctionNames,  :
  Dynamic indexing found in a vector of indices, t:47. Only scalar indices, such as 'idx' in 'x[idx]', can be dynamic. One can instead use dynamic indexing in a vector of indices inside a nimbleFunction.

Thanks,

Katie

Hi Katie,
Thanks for posting the question and welcome to nimble.
It looks like the index range "t:n.years" appears in a context where t is not defined. That made nimble think you plan for t to be a variable in the model and to error out with a message about what it looks like you are trying to do. Although sometimes the message isn't correct (because it's a guess based on why this error often can occur), the clue about "t:47" made me look at where that appears.
HTH,
Perry

messages.subject: Re: BNP AR(1) model
messages.body_plain:
hi Mostafa,

The CRP sampling we have set up is written under the assumption that either observations or random effects are clustered into discrete clusters and are conditionally independent of each other, which doesn't fit with the autoregressive structure you have.

I'm not understanding the details of how you're setting up your model, but for this kind of structure, I would suggest using the stickbreaking representation rather than the CRP. In the NIMBLE manual in the chapter on BNP, you should see some discussion of that.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

Thanks for creating this branch! The code did run and produce sample cluster assignments. However, when I run the joint clusters (both z[i] and y[j]) on real data, one dimension always clusters everything into just 1-2 clusters for every single sample. The other dimension produces a broader range of clusters that vary from sample to sample. For example, every sample will set the y values to the same cluster for all y[i] elements, while the z values will be different for each sample.

If I update the code to only cluster responses along a single dimension than I get more reasonable clusters for each dimension, which suggests that something is going on with sampling when there are two dimensions. It's like the samples get stuck on a particular cluster assignment and never leave it. It's also possible that this is a data size issue and I may just not have enough samples to justify multi-dimensional clustering like this.

In the short run I ended up finding another way to look at these data, so this is now more of an academic issue than a practical one. If this is something that is of interest to your team to resolve for future users I'd be happy to continue to explore what's happening here, but I'm also happy to just leave this where it is for now and call the issue closed.

Either way, thank you so much for your help!

messages.subject: Re: backwards indexing
messages.body_plain:
Dear Nour,
Thanks for posting a question. Did you mean to attach a file?
Backwards indexing sometimes arises when the indices come from (constant) variables, e.g.
for(i in 1:N) {
  for(j in start[i]:end[i]) {
    <some code>
 }
}
then if start[i] > end[i], there will be a backwards indexing warning. That's just a guess of how it can arise.

The non-constant indices warning can arise if those z elements are used as nested indices, e.g.
x[ z[1, 1, 1] ]
Then nimbleModel checks to see if z was provided via the constants list (as opposed to the data list) and is saying that if the z values are not going to change then it is better to provide them via constants so nimbleModel can take advantage of that. Again that is just a guess at what might trigger the warning.

But anyway please send along your code if those points don't resolve your questions.
Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Brennan,

I took another look at this. It's been a bit hard to keep track of all the details here, so the following may be incomplete, but it's my current understanding:

1) Be careful about your initial values for theta. If you draw those from a beta or Dirichlet when you have a value of alpha near 0 (e.g., resulting in values of `ab` of, say, (0.1, 0.1)), it's very easy to get initial theta values that are very, very close to 0 and of exactly 1.0. These can then cause sampling issues. I suggesting initializing the theta values so they are somewhere in (0.05, 0.95) and not close to 0 or 1.
2) I think my suggestion to use truncation is not helpful as that can itself cause numerical issues when we normalize the truncated density based on using the distribution's CDF. So I suggest avoiding that.
3) I believe that if you re-install nimble from the `crp_underflow` branch, you will no longer get crashes. I tested this with having the `beta` parameter values either from a Beta or a Dirichlet and the `theta` parameter values from a Beta, and the MCMC seemed to run. Mixing is not necessarily good, though I didn't look at it carefully.
4) Using the Dirichlet for both `beta` and `theta` should now run. However you'll see warnings about "values of infinity for the log probability density corresponding to multiple potential cluster memberships". This occurs when sampling `z[i]` when the chain has a `theta[i,1:2]` value in which one value is exactly 1 and the other is exactly 0 or very close to 0. In the CRP sampling, when the `ab[i,1:2]` values are sufficiently small, this can result in the log probability overflowing and giving Infinity. This can happen for multiple possible `z[i]` values, so I don't think the MCMC will be valid. One possible work-around is to avoid having nimble using the conjugate sampler for the thetas. I think this would prevent getting theta values that are so close to (or equal to) 0 and 1, but I haven't tried it.

At a higher level, I think much of the cause of what is going on is that the model structure places density on values of alpha (and therefore elements of `ab`) near 0. This allows very extreme values of theta (very near or equal to 0 or 1). And that leads to the numerical issues. Note that a uniform distribution is the same as a Beta(1,1) or Dirichlet(1,1,...,1)). Having parameter values much less than 1 in a Beta or Dirichlet results in an unusual "u-shaped" distribution where most of the mass is near 0 and 1.

-chris

> > > > > It looks like there is another related, but distinct, numerical issue that can come up in this case. What I am seeing is that when one of the two `ab[i,1:2]` values gets close to zero, numerical underflow can cause a sampled value of `theta[i,1:2]` (from its conjugate Dirichlet distribution) to be exactly (1,0) (or (0,1)). Then if that `theta[i,1:2]` is the only member of its cluster, when the CRP sampling goes to sample a new value for `z[i]`, it's possible that the log probability density value for `theta[i,1:2]` under the other clusters are all -Inf. And using the non-conjugate CRP sampler to sample `alpha[i]` and `beta[i,1:2]` values for a new cluster will generally give values that also have -Inf for the log probability density value for `theta[i,1:2]`. At that point, the CRP sampler is trying to decide between the various possible new values for `z[i]` with all the log probabilities being -Inf and the crash occurs.
> > > > >
> > > > > This is a tricky situation. We can of course (and will at a minimum in our upcoming release) error trap this and produce an error message rather than a crash.
> > > > >

And I don't see a reasonable way to avoid getting exact (1,0) values in the conjugate sampling of `theta[i,1:2]`.

> > > > >
> > > > > You could also think about using the stickbreaking representation rather than the CRP.  That might avoid the issue. Or it seems that in the paper you reference, they used some other sampling strategies based on drawing from the prior.

messages.subject: Parallel processing without repeat NIMBLE compilation
messages.subject_clean: Parallel processing without repeat NIMBLE compilation
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I hope you are doing well,

Me and my colleagues have been modelling species occupancy within a HPC environment. In the past, we have used JAGS to fit models separately for each species within a taxonomic group, distributing them across nodes. A major challenge for us is that when we attempt to fit models for larger taxonomic groups (which have many species and, therefore, require many nodes), we exceed the wall time, and our job is cancelled.

We are exploring transitioning to NIMBLE, but we're worried about having the same issue that we currently face with JAGS. We would like to know if efficiency can be improved by avoiding recompilation of the NIMBLE model across nodes. My hope is that we can compile it once using occupancy data for the first species, then within separate nodes, set the data to the species being modelled, before running the MCMC.

Is this approach feasible? I've see in discussions in past years that saving a compiled NIMBLE model is not possible (with plans for it's implementation). Is this still the case? If so, do you have any advice about how we could improve our efficiency in our circumstance?

Thanks for your time, and apologies for my basic knowledge on HPC and NIMBLE - I'm very new to both! Please let me know if any information I have provided needs more explanation.

All the best,

Dylan

> > > > >
> > > > > Regarding your second question: If by "ignores their gradient evaluation" you mean "ignores the gradient evaluation of the custom-written nimble functions entirely", then no, gradients of these functions are not ignored, but rather algebraically derived (via automatic differentiation), while using the values of the constant arguments you provided. messages.subject: Allowing an individual variable to depend on state in CR model
messages.subject_clean: Allowing an individual variable to depend on state in CR model
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I’m trying to build a multistate capture-recapture (CR) model in which:

-        A quantitative individual variable (noted X, e.g. date of migration) between year t and t+1 is allowed to differ depending on the state in year t

-        One of the components of the transition probabilities from year t to year t+1 depends on X.

For most individuals, X is not available and is thus imputed.

The CR model works fine and produces reasonable results when the quantitative variables X depends on age and environmental covariates.

When X is allowed to depend on the state in year t (or at least that I try to do so), the model runs fine, but the results are somewhat surprising:  the posteriors of estimated differences in X depending on state are very narrow and centered on 0. Given the limited amount of data available, even if the differences in X between states are truly null, I expected that the posteriors would be much wider. I’m also unsure how to allow X to depend on state. Below is how I tried (omitting the effects of age and environmental covariates):

Let betai,t,k be the component of the transition probability (from t to t+1) that depends on Xi,t. k refers to the state in which individual i is in year t. Assuming there are two states k:

For the first state:

logit(beta[i, t, 1]) <- b[1] +

                                    b[2] * X[i, t, 1]

mu_X[i, t, 1] <- x[1]

X[i, t, 1] ~ dnorm(mu_X[i, t, 1], sd = sigma)

For the second state:

logit(beta[i, t, 2]) <- b[1] +

                                    b[2] * X[i, t, 2]

mu_X[i, t, 2] <- x[1] +  x[2]

 X[i, t, 2] ~ dnorm(mu_X[i, t, 2], sd = sigma)

Note that X[i, t, 1] and X[i, t, 2] are the same: a matrix with as many lines as there are marked individuals, and as many columns as there are years, mostly filled with NAs, with only some individuals in some years for which X is known.

This way of specifying the model seems odd to me, but I couldn’t think of another way of allowing X to depend on state. I guess the fact that  X[i, t, 1] and X[i, t, 2]  are the same explains why the estimate of x[2] is so narrowly centered on 0.

What am I doing wrong here?

Attached is a simulated dataset (where x[2] = 1.5), the code of my CR model, and the fit of the model.

Thanks in advance,

Marwan

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dylan,

Unfortunately, this is still a limitation of NIMBLE. As you mentioned, we've had plans to make saving and reloading compiled objects possible, and have made real progress on that for what will become NIMBLE 2.0, but it's still work in progress.

There are various tricks one can use to reduce the number of nodes in the model and also the number of the MCMC samplers that are created, which can often reduce compilation time. So if you wanted to share your model code (simply sharing the model code and the values of any constants that indicate the sizes of various variables), I or someone else on the list might be able to make some suggestions.

-chris

> Me and my colleagues have been modelling species occupancy within a HPC environment. In the past, we have used JAGS to fit models separately for each species within a taxonomic group, distributing them across nodes. A major challenge for us is that when we attempt to fit models for larger taxonomic groups (which have many species and, therefore, require many nodes), we exceed the wall time, and our job is cancelled.
>
> We are exploring transitioning to NIMBLE, but we're worried about having the same issue that we currently face with JAGS. We would like to know if efficiency can be improved by avoiding recompilation of the NIMBLE model across nodes. My hope is that we can compile it once using occupancy data for the first species, then within separate nodes, set the data to the species being modelled, before running the MCMC.
>
> Is this approach feasible? I've see in discussions in past years that saving a compiled NIMBLE model is not possible (with plans for it's implementation). Is this still the case? If so, do you have any advice about how we could improve our efficiency in our circumstance?
>
> Thanks for your time, and apologies for my basic knowledge on HPC and NIMBLE - I'm very new to both! Please let me know if any information I have provided needs more explanation.
>
> All the best,
>
> Dylan

messages.body_plain:
Hi Marwan,

I'm having trouble understanding a few things in your description:

1) Does each individual in each year have their own state? If so, what variable in your model represents that state? You index `x` by state (1 or 2) but I don't see in your email where you denote the unknown state. I would think there should be something like `s[i,t]` that is a discrete variable taking possible values 1,2,...,max_number_states.
2) When you talk about transition probabilities, these are the probabilities of going from one state at time `t` to another state at time `t+1`, right? Is the 'state' that relates to the transition probabilities the same state you are talking about? If so, I would think you would have `beta[i, t, k1, k2]` indicating the probability of going from state k1 at time t to state k2 at time t+1 for individual i.
3) I would think that an individual in year t would have a single unknown migration date, i.e., X[i,t] rather than X[i,t,k]. That date might have a different distribution depending on the state the individual is in. Just to give an example, perhaps `X[i,t] ~ dnorm(mu_X[s[i,t]], sd=sigma)` where `s[i,t]` is the state of individual i in year t.

My suggestions above are not meant to be concrete suggestions of how to change the model but just ideas to try to help think through what you are trying to do here.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
Dear Miki,

Thanks for posting the question and welcome to nimble.

I think there might be some basics for you to get up to speed on about nimble models. The model code declares relationships among nodes in a directed acyclic graph. For you coming from Stan, this is quite different. Stan and most programming involves step-by-step instructions, re-using variables and so on (imperative programming). nimble's model language is declarative. That means the code is processed to determine the known set of relationships among nodes, and the order of declarations does not matter. For this reason, if-then-else is not supported (well it is supported but in a different way, to include or exclude blocks of code for the entire model, not differently for iterations in a for loop). And a node can't be declared twice, such as "num_inf <- 1" and later "num_inf <- num_inf + 1". That would mean the same node appears in the model graph twice, which can't happen. num_inf (or any other node) can only have one declared relationship. nimble's algorithms can then use the DAG relationships in setting up calculations.

Sometimes, what people want to do with if-then-else can instead be achieved by nested indexing. e.g.
for(i in 1:n) {
  x[k[i]] <- {some equation}
}
where k[i] is provided in the constants list and determines in advance which of the x[i] should have this declaration.

In your case, while I am not trying to follow your code in full detail, it appears that the for loop iterations are more involved. In that case, you can put them in a nimbleFunction and use that in the model. For example, you could replace the entire nested for loops with

infection[1:N, t_start:t_end] ~ d_my_model_log_probs(delta1, delta2, alpha, beta )

Then in the nimbleFunction d_my_model_log_probs you would calculate the sum of log probabilities of all the infection[,] data using your for loops. We call this a user-defined distribution.

At this point I'll encourage you to look up user-defined distributions in our user manual at r-nimble.org <http://r-nimble.org>. After you've explored more, feel free to ask more.

Perry
